t: #3400 Maximum Number of Matching Indices After Right Shifts
o: Try every shift s ∈ [0, n): shifting nums1 right by s aligns nums1[(i+s) mod n] with nums2[i]; count matches and take the maximum. With n ≤ 3000, the O(n²) brute force (~9M comparisons) is perfectly fine. Example 1: shift 2 makes the arrays identical → 6 matches.
k: There are only n distinct shifts, and each is checked in O(n) — O(n²) total is acceptable at n = 3000.
Equivalently, for each value match between nums1[i] and nums2[j], the implied shift is (j − i) mod n; tally shifts in a hashmap, which is much faster when values are near-distinct.

a.i: Direct simulation of the definition: for each shift amount, count aligned equalities with modular indexing.
s: For s from 0 to n−1, count i with nums1[(i+s) mod n] == nums2[i].
a.t: O(n²) — n shifts × n comparisons each; ~9×10^6 operations at n = 3000.

a.n: Approach 2: Shift Tally via Hash Map
a.i: Index nums2's values, then for every pair (i in nums1, j in nums2) with equal values, vote for shift (j − i) mod n; the most-voted shift is the answer. Worst case still O(n²) with heavy duplication, but near-linear when values are mostly distinct.
s: Build value → list of indices in nums2.
For each i and each j with nums2[j] == nums1[i], increment counter[(j − i) mod n].
Return the maximum counter value (0 if no equal values exist).
a.t: O(n²) worst case (all values equal) but O(n + m) expected for near-distinct values, where m is the number of value matches.

w: Lead with the brute force (it meets the constraints comfortably) and mention the hashmap variant as the optimization interviewers probe for. Pitfalls: getting the shift direction right ((j − i) mod n vs (i − j)), negative modulo in C++/Java/JS, and early-exiting when all n match. Follow-up: allow left shifts too (symmetric), or circular-rotation matching with string algorithms (KMP/FFT) for very large n.
